openingProblem.problem: Between 1930 and 1983 Argentina had 25 presidents and 22 years of military rule. Between 1983 and 1999 it held four presidential elections, survived four military revolts and two economic collapses, and in 1999 the governing party handed over power peacefully. Did Argentine democracy consolidate, or merely survive?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: consolidated or merely survived?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Justice and its limits: the Trial of the Juntas, 1985
chunks.body:
Alfonsín's government set out to do what no Latin American democracy had done before: put the leaders of the previous dictatorship on trial in a civilian court. The **Trial of the Juntas** opened on 22 April 1985. The prosecutors, Julio César Strassera and Luis Moreno Ocampo, presented 709 cases, of which 280 were heard, and 833 witnesses testified. It was the first major trial of its kind since Nuremberg and Tokyo after the Second World War.

On **9 December 1985** the court sentenced General Jorge Videla and Admiral Emilio Massera to life imprisonment. General Roberto Viola received seventeen years, and two other commanders shorter terms. Four were acquitted, including Galtieri, though he was court-martialled separately for the conduct of the Falklands war.

At the same time Alfonsín faced an economic emergency. When he took office, inflation was nearly 30 per cent a month and the country was close to default. He warned that democracy had little to offer "unless the economic question is definitely resolved". In 1985 his minister Juan Sourrouille launched the **Austral plan**: prices and wages were frozen, money printing stopped, and a new currency, the austral, replaced the peso. Inflation fell at once, and the governing UCR won the 1985 midterm elections.

This mattered because 1985 was the high point of Alfonsín's presidency, which meant that democracy appeared able to deliver both justice and economic stability, for a time.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Trial of the Juntas was a landmark in justice.
The Austral plan brought a brief recovery.

useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that a civilian court had judged a former dictatorship, so the principle that no one stood above the law was established.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, four commanders were acquitted, and hundreds of lower-ranking officers still awaited trial.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The trial was therefore a landmark in justice that also raised the question of how far prosecutions could go.

chunks.title: Military pressure: Full Stop, Due Obedience and the Carapintadas, 1986–1990
chunks.body:
Prosecutions did not stop with the junta leaders. Hundreds of other officers faced charges, and the armed forces grew restless. On **24 December 1986** Congress passed the **Full Stop Law**, which limited prosecutions to those indicted within sixty days.

The army's anger erupted at Easter 1987. On **15 April** Lieutenant Colonel Aldo Rico led an uprising of the **Carapintadas** ("painted faces") at the Campo de Mayo infantry school, demanding an end to the trials. Some 200,000 people gathered at the presidential palace to defend democracy, and Alfonsín went in person to negotiate with the rebels, who surrendered on 19 April. But on **4 June 1987** Congress passed the **Law of Due Obedience**, which in effect exempted officers below the rank of colonel from punishment because they had been obeying orders. Many human rights groups saw it as a concession to the remnants of authoritarian rule.

Further revolts followed in January and December 1988; after the second, the government conceded some of the rebels' demands. Menem, who became president in 1989, went further. In October 1989 he pardoned 39 military men held for crimes of the dictatorship and 164 Carapintadas. After a last, violent uprising on 3 December 1990, which loyal forces crushed within 36 hours, he pardoned the most important people convicted for the crimes of the Dirty War, including the junta leaders.

This mattered because military pressure narrowed justice step by step, which meant that by 1990 democracy had survived but most of those responsible for the repression were free.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Menem's pardons completed the retreat from justice.

useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that most officers below the rank of colonel could no longer be punished, so justice was limited to a handful of leaders.

useItInAnEssay.judge: Democracy therefore survived the military, but at the cost of justice for most victims.

chunks.title: Hyperinflation and the Menem revolution, 1989–1995
chunks.body:
The Austral plan did not last. Provinces and state enterprises ran deficits, the government began printing money again, and inflation returned in 1986. The UCR lost the 1987 midterm elections, and by 1989 inflation had turned into **hyperinflation**, with riots in the streets. The Peronist **Carlos Menem** won the presidential election of 14 May 1989. Alfonsín resigned and handed over power on **8 July 1989**, five months early. The US Congressional Research Service nonetheless credits Alfonsín with restoring democratic institutions.

Menem surprised his own party. He broke with Peronist protectionism and, in the words of the CRS, transformed Argentina "from a state-dominated protectionist economy to one committed to free market principles". Most state enterprises were privatized. In 1991 his economy minister, **Domingo Cavallo**, introduced **Convertibility**, a law fixing the peso one-to-one to the US dollar and limiting the printing of money. Hyperinflation was eliminated and the early 1990s brought growth. Argentina restored diplomatic relations with Britain and became a close partner of the United States.

There were costs. Large numbers of workers in privatized enterprises lost their jobs, and unemployment rose above 10 per cent. The currency board left Argentina exposed to fiscal deficits, high foreign debt and an overvalued peso.

This mattered because Menem's reforms ended hyperinflation and gave democracy economic credibility, which meant that his government won popular support even as inequality and unemployment grew.

useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the economy stabilised and grew in the early 1990s, so Menem gained the popularity to win again in 1995.

chunks.title: A new constitution and a peaceful handover, 1993–1999
chunks.body:
Menem wanted a second term, which the constitution forbade. In the **Pact of Olivos** of 17 November 1993 he and Alfonsín agreed on a constitutional reform: the UCR would support one presidential re-election, and in exchange Menem accepted measures to limit presidential power, including a four-year term, a third senator for each province, a Council of Magistracy to oversee judges, and an autonomous government for Buenos Aires.

A constituent assembly elected in April 1994 approved the reform on **22 August 1994**. International human rights treaties were given constitutional status. The president would be elected directly, with a run-off. The doctrine that had legitimised *de facto* governments was repealed: any break in constitutional order was declared illegal, and citizens were given the right to resist a coup. An ombudsman was created.

Menem was re-elected in May 1995. His critics called his government authoritarian, claiming that it weakened Congress and the judiciary; the Supreme Court had been filled with his supporters. Corruption charges multiplied, and the bombings of the Israeli embassy in 1992 and of the AMIA Jewish community centre in 1994, which killed 85 people, remained unsolved.

Yet democracy held. On **24 October 1999** Fernando de la Rúa of the UCR-led Alliance won the presidency with 48.5 per cent, defeating the Peronists amid anger over corruption and unemployment. It was the fourth presidential election since 1983. The CRS called Argentina's return to stable civilian rule "remarkable" for a country that had seen 25 presidents and 22 years of military rule between 1930 and 1983.

This mattered because elections and a reformed constitution survived economic crisis, military revolts and a dominant president, which meant that by 1999 democracy had been consolidated in its institutions, if not in public trust.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Menem's rule weakened checks and balances.

howItGetsAsked: Examine the reasons for, and the results of, Argentina's constitutional reform between 1993 and 1999.
To what extent had democracy been consolidated in Argentina between 1983 and 1999?

useItInAnEssay.claim: The 1994 reform both strengthened democratic rules and served Menem's ambition.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Under the Pact of Olivos, Menem gained the right to one re-election, while the reform declared any break in constitutional order illegal and gave human rights treaties constitutional status.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that future coups were outlawed, so the constitution itself now defended democracy.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, critics claimed Menem weakened Congress and the judiciary, and the Supreme Court was filled with his supporters.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The reform therefore strengthened democracy's rules more than the practice of checks and balances.

segments.text: Alfonsín's presidency ended early because his government could not control deficits.
The Austral plan of 1985 froze prices and wages and stopped money printing, but provinces and state enterprises kept running deficits, and inflation returned in 1986.
This meant that the government began printing money again, so by 1989 inflation turned into hyperinflation and riots.
However, Alfonsín had inherited near-default and inflation of nearly 30 per cent a month from the military, which limited what any government could do.
The failure to control deficits was therefore the decisive reason, worsened by the debts left by the dictatorship.

essayQuestions.text: To what extent had democracy been consolidated in Argentina between 1983 and 1999?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far

modelPlan.thesis: Democracy was consolidated in its institutions, since military revolts failed, power changed hands peacefully in 1989 and 1999, and the 1994 constitution outlawed coups; but justice for past crimes and checks on presidential power remained weak.
modelPlan.counter: The CRS calls the return to stable civilian rule 'remarkable' given Argentina's history.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Consolidated or survived? Consolidated in institutions; incomplete in justice and accountability.

segments.text: By 1999 Argentine democracy had been consolidated in its institutions, if not in its practice.
Power passed between parties in 1989 and 1999, the last military revolt was crushed in 1990, and the 1994 constitution declared any break in constitutional order illegal.
This meant that the cycle of coups that had produced 25 presidents between 1930 and 1983 had been broken.
However, the amnesty laws and pardons left most perpetrators free, and critics claimed Menem weakened Congress and the courts.
Democracy had therefore consolidated as a system of government, while justice and accountability remained incomplete.

essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast how Argentina and South Africa dealt with the crimes of their former regimes between 1983 and 1998.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences throughout
decodeKey.factorOrTask: Dealing with the crimes of former regimes
decodeKey.judgement: Truth, justice, or stability: which did each achieve?

modelPlan.thesis: Argentina began with retributive justice, trying and convicting the junta leaders, but military pressure forced amnesty laws and pardons; South Africa chose restorative justice from the start, exchanging amnesty for truth; both left most perpetrators unpunished, but South Africa gained more truth with less conflict.

arguments.claim: Difference: trials versus a truth commission.
Difference: how far the truth was heard.

modelPlan.counter: Argentina's trials established that former rulers could be judged by a civilian court, which South Africa's amnesty did not.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which approach achieved more? South Africa's for truth and stability; Argentina's, briefly, for justice.

segments.text: Argentina and South Africa took opposite approaches to the crimes of their former regimes, but ended with similar limits.
Argentina's Trial of the Juntas sentenced Videla and Massera to life in December 1985, whereas South Africa's TRC, based on restorative justice, heard more than 22,000 victims in 1996–98.
This meant that Argentina pursued punishment and provoked military revolts, while South Africa exchanged amnesty for full disclosure and avoided confrontation with its security forces.
However, in both states most perpetrators went unpunished: Argentina's Due Obedience law and Menem's pardons freed them, while in South Africa many victims felt justice had not been done.
The two approaches therefore differed in method, but South Africa's produced more truth with less risk to democracy.
